Nov 20 : Hackers this week breached a system that the US Department of Agriculture uses to send payments to farmers, NBC News reported on Friday, citing two former USDA officials with knowledge of the matter. The department notified employees of the incident on Thursday, the former officials told NBC. While the payments database is the known extent of the intrusion so far, the former officials warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety data and research on animal-borne illnesses, according to the report. It is not known who was responsible. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions to the USDA, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Source: Reuters

Nov 20 : CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire rival cybersecurity provider Zscaler amid consolidation in the security software sector, according to two people familiar with the matter. The talks between the two companies are ongoing, the sources said. No deal is guaranteed, and the discussions could still end without an agreement, the people added. Shares of Zscaler, which has a market capitalization of about $32 billion as of Friday's close, jumped 17 per cent in after-hours trading. CrowdStrike shares fell 8 per cent. A combination would create one of the world's largest pure-play cybersecurity providers as enterprise customers seek to reduce the number of security vendors they use, favoring providers that can deliver multiple products through a single relationship.

CrowdStrike and Zscaler did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. CrowdStrike's Falcon platform is widely used to secure endpoints such as laptops, servers and mobile devices, while Zscaler specializes in cloud-based network security services that help companies securely connect users to applications without relying on traditional corporate networks. Founded in 2011 by chief executive George Kurtz, CrowdStrike has grown into one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies, helping organizations detect and respond to cyber threats through its cloud-native software platform. The Austin, Texas-based company has expanded beyond endpoint protection through acquisitions and internal development into areas including cloud, identity and threat intelligence security. The deal would address one of CrowdStrike's biggest gaps in network security and help it compete more directly with platform providers such as Palo Alto Networks. Zscaler, founded in 2007 by chief executive Jay Chaudhry, pioneered zero-trust security, which continuously verifies users and devices before granting access to corporate applications and data. Its cloud-based software lets employees securely access applications from any location. Any transaction would likely require the backing of Chaudhry, who remains Zscaler's largest shareholder. The discussions come as cybersecurity companies race to expand offerings to meet demand for integrated platforms that address a wider range of threats. Zscaler's shares fell sharply earlier this year in a broader software selloff as investors weighed the impact of artificial intelligence, but have since rebounded. Bloomberg News first reported on the merger discussion.

Source: Reuters

Nov 20 : Coding startup Cognition AI is in funding talks at a $75 billion valuation, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The company is considering raising $2 billion or more in the latest round, the report said, adding that the talks were ongoing and the details could change. The news comes about two months after Cognition raised $2 billion in a Series E funding round at a valuation of $48 billion. The round was led by new investors Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, alongside existing backers Founders Fund, General Catalyst, and Avenir. Cognition did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The company is an AI startup that develops autonomous software-engineering agents, which can plan, write, test and deploy code with limited human intervention. The company was valued at $26 billion in a funding round in May, when it raised $1 billion.

Source: Reuters

Nov 20 : The US Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday proposed taking direct control of a comprehensive industry-funded market surveillance tool long the subject of cost and privacy complaints, the agency announced. The proposal makes good on the Trump administration's pledge to rework the so-called Consolidated Audit Trail, which the agency first mandated following the 2010 "flash crash," in which Wall Street indices temporarily erased nearly $1 trillion in market value in minutes. The surveillance system remains the only source of its kind for comprehensive, real-time data and information about market events — allowing regulators to reconstruct every order, route and execution for US-listed equities and options nationwide — making it crucial to investigations into possible market misconduct including insider trading and market manipulation. But investment industry and stock market operators have battled over who should foot the bill for its development and operations costs while conservative critics earlier decried what they said was the CAT's invasive collection of personal data.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins said in Friday's statement the changes would make the CAT "accountable in its governance and disciplined in its costs," to the benefit of both exchange operators and market participants. The system is currently operated by an organization overseen by the industry-funded Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. SEC officials told reporters on Friday the CAT's current annual operating costs were down about 45 per cent since 2024 to $137 million. But under Friday's proposal, stock exchanges and broker-dealers themselves would collect and report the same data to the agency or its designee, giving the SEC direct control, the agency said. The new rules would also subject the system's costs to annual funding legislation from Congress, something market operators and others warn could expose it to government shutdowns. The agency earlier this year eliminated the systematic collection and storage of traders' personal information such as names, addresses and dates of birth. The announcement confirmed that the Trump administration had stepped back from conservatives' most aggressive moves. The manifesto known as "Project 2025," to which Atkins was a contributor, called for the CAT's outright elimination. The proposal is subject to a 60-day public comment period prior to any decision on whether to adopt a final version.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 20 : Honda said on Friday it is recalling 810,592 older cars and SUVs in the US over a risk that Takata air bag inflators could rupture. The recall includes some 2013 Honda Accord, 2012-2013 Honda Civic, 2012-2013 Honda CR-V, 2013 Acura ILX and 2013 Acura RDX vehicles that were originally sold or registered in 14 states or territories known for high temperature, humidity and large temperature fluctuations. Honda said there no injuries or crashes tied to the vehicles being recalled, and there have been no air bag inflator ruptures. But the company's long-term monitoring and analysis revealed potential propellant degradation in certain inflators within specific geographic regions, it said. There have been at least 28 deaths in the United States stemming from defective Takata air bag inflators since 2009, an issue that prompted the largest auto recall in US history.

Over the past decade, two dozen major automakers have recalled more than 100 million vehicles fitted with Takata airbag inflators worldwide, including about 67 million vehicles in the United States. Various automakers have also reported hundreds of injuries in vehicles since 2009 from Takata air bag inflators that can explode, unleashing metal shrapnel inside cars and trucks, killing or injuring drivers or other vehicle occupants. The vehicles in the new recall have air bags inflators that contain a moisture-absorbing material — unlike the millions of vehicles recalled previously. The recall applies to vehicles sold or registered in Alabama, California, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands, Northern Mariana Islands (Saipan), Guam and American Samoa.

Nov 20 : CONMEBOL on Friday reaffirmed its unanimous support for Gianni Infantino's bid for another term as FIFA president, with all 10 member associations of the South American confederation backing his candidacy ahead of next year's election. The endorsement was confirmed after a meeting of CONMEBOL's council in Barranquilla, Colombia, where the organisation said its members had reiterated their "firm support" for Infantino. "That is a recognition of the leadership of the current FIFA president and the positive transformations in football," CONMEBOL said in a statement. Infantino, who has led world soccer's governing body since 2016, is seeking a fourth term in the election scheduled for March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.

It will be Infantino's first contested re-election after he was returned unopposed in 2023. The CONMEBOL endorsement follows support announced by the Union of Arab Football Associations (UAFA) on Thursday. The organisation, which represents 22 national football associations across Africa and Asia, said its backing recognised Infantino's contribution to the development of the game. Infantino has faced calls to resign since the collapse of his FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, which sought to bring private investors into a new commercial entity controlling rights linked to major competitions, including the World Cup. The proposal prompted opposition from several confederations and European associations, with the French federation withdrawing its support for Infantino and Diallo emerging as UEFA's preferred candidate. The election will be held at the FIFA Congress in Morocco on March 18.

WASHINGTON, Nov 20 : Alphabet's self-driving unit Waymo said on Friday it is issuing two recalls for its robotaxis over incidents involving closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control. Earlier this week, Waymo said it halted operations of its vehicles on US freeways, after a California regulator barred its vehicles from freeways in the state. The California ban, which took effect last week, is a result of a series of incidents where Waymo robotaxis entered active construction zones, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said. Waymo said a statement it filed two safety recalls with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Thursday on its automated driving system "to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control."

The closed freeway lanes recall stems from unusual circumstances where a Waymo vehicle may enter and continue driving in a closed freeway lane, the company said, adding it is still working on the recall remedy. Waymo said there were no collisions or injuries reported from the closed freeway events. The manual traffic recall is to ensure self-driving vehicles better responds to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or other emergency personnel and follows a collision in which a Waymo followed directions from an officer, but the officer was then temporarily obstructed. That update was completed on November 6. Waymo says its technology outperforms statistically comparable human benchmarks and drastically reduces injury-causing crashes. Last week, NHTSA said it opened a recall query into Waymo vehicles after numerous incidents of its robotaxis passing stopped school buses. The probe will look into nearly 3,000 company-owned self-driving vehicles. Investigators want to determine whether a software update Waymo rolled out late last year failed to stop its driverless cars from passing school buses with flashing red lights. Most of the violations happened after the company said the remedy had been deployed. Separately, NHTSA and the National Transportation Safety Board have opened probes after one of Waymo's self-driving vehicles struck a child in January near an elementary school in Santa Monica, California.

Source: Reuters

Nov 20 : Ford, Honda, Stellantis' FCA unit and Volkswagen sued New Jersey on Friday to block a new state law they say increases the amounts automakers must pay franchised dealers for warranty and recall repairs. In a complaint filed in federal court in Trenton, New Jersey, the automakers said the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Open Recall Notice and Fair Compensation Act gives dealers a "blank check" to set prices for warranty, recall and other repair services, while prohibiting manufacturers from avoiding "extortionate" results or recovering the costs. New Jersey's law will shift more than $375 million a year to dealers from automakers, giving dealers a "windfall" by imposing no obligation to use the money to improve customer service or boost compensation for employees, the automakers said. "In short, the act rewards dealers for charging their customers more," the automakers said.

The office of New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, who enforces the state's laws, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. New Jersey's law took effect on April 1, after former Governor Phil Murphy signed it in September 2025. CONSTITUTIONAL VIOLATIONS ALLEGED The automakers objected to letting dealers charge a "labor multiplier" based on samples of repair orders, saying it lets dealers bill for substantially more labor time than they actually work. They also challenged provisions requiring automakers to pay marked-up prices on parts that the dealers received at reduced cost or for free, and preventing automakers from providing less expensive parts even if supply, demand or other factors justified price cuts. Ford, Honda, FCA — which includes Fiat and Chrysler — and Volkswagen said that since the law took effect, each has received dozens of bills requiring payment "for hours that no technician works, that surpass what comparable dealers charge for the same work, and that exceed what retail customers pay." They said the law violates the US Constitution's Commerce Clause and Takings Clause, is preempted by federal law governing recalls, and violates New Jersey's Constitution. The nonprofit New Jersey Coalition of Automotive Retailers is also a defendant. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Source: Reuters
